say: We're returning to the same fictional hotel, but today the coordinator needs to improve how the team works rather than simply manage the next message. We'll turn several imperfect documents into a practical readiness guide for the next conference.

Keep your own guide at the centre of the exercise, because the illustrated results aren't a document to copy. What matters is whether a busy colleague could use your output without mistaking an idea or a gap for a confirmed instruction.
welcome.ask: What makes a guide useful during a busy shift rather than merely pleasant to read?
welcome.watch: Introduce the continuity with the inbox workshop without assuming every learner attended it.

say: The manager's request comes after a conference where several things went wrong, and the coordinator needs to capture what should happen differently next time. Relying on someone's memory won't give the next shift a dependable way to prepare.

Our answer will be a readiness guide, not a claim that every problem has already been solved. As we work, we'll preserve confirmed requirements and make missing approvals, contacts, and decisions visible rather than quietly filling them in.
request.ask: What information would the next shift need that might be lost if the team relied only on memory?
request.watch: Keep the manager's request framed as improving a working document, not inventing hotel policy.

say: This route starts with finding the context and checking the evidence before we draft anything. Then we'll improve the guide, review it against the files, and reuse the checked content in a visual.

The order matters because polishing an unsupported instruction can make it more persuasive without making it more reliable. Notice that critique and review have their own place in the workflow; they aren't simply requests to make the writing sound nicer.
flow.ask: Why do we check the source material before asking for a new guide?
flow.watch: Trace the six moves; explain that the actual exercise reviews the guide before demonstrating visual reuse.

say: Use the three labels on this screen to orient yourself in the exercise: Word is where the working guide will live, Create is the visual demonstration, and the work-context route connects our questions to the selected training files. We don't need to explore every feature behind those names today.
The practical distinction is between gathering evidence, writing the output, and reusing it in another format. Whichever route we're using, the confirmed meaning must stay intact.
ideas.ask: Which part of today's work gathers evidence, and which part produces the guide colleagues will use?
ideas.watch: Explain the workshop roles only; don't turn the screen into an unsourced product-capability overview.

say: Check that you can open the work environment for the chat and Word exercises and that you have the four practice files available. We'll use the same fictional pack throughout, so there's no need to bring in a real hotel document.

If Create isn't available on your device, you can watch my demonstration of the final visual. Tell me about missing access now so you can spend the session making decisions about the guide rather than searching for controls.
needs.ask: Can you follow the chat and Word exercises yourself, or do you need the demonstration route?
needs.watch: Check live access and file availability; identify anyone following the Create demo rather than creating an output.

say: Download the four training documents, individually or as the pack, and keep them together. They deliberately include different kinds of evidence: an event brief, an issues report, informal handover notes, and a weak checklist.

Don't tidy or rewrite them during setup, because their differences are part of the exercise. We're going to learn how to use a mixed source pack without turning every statement into an equally authoritative instruction.
get.ask: Have you downloaded all four source documents without changing their contents?
get.watch: Check the four filenames; distinguish the weak source checklist from the new guide learners will create.

say: For the route demonstrated in this workshop, create the Conference Day folder in your work OneDrive and place all four source documents there. Keeping them together makes it easier to choose the correct evidence when the prompts ask for files.
Open the folder and confirm the uploads before leaving this step. A downloaded file on your computer and a file available through the workshop's selection route aren't the same setup state.
folder.ask: Can you see all four source documents in your Conference Day folder?
folder.watch: Verify the actual folder contents; avoid repeating the page's broad claim about every possible file-reading method.

say: Give each document a role before asking Copilot to combine them: the brief carries confirmed event requirements, the issues report records what happened, and the handover notes contain informal suggestions. The draft checklist is the existing output we'll critique later.
Those roles stop a helpful suggestion from becoming an invented policy. We'll begin with the first three files and only add the weak checklist when we reach the critique exercise.
files.ask: Which file would you consult to distinguish a confirmed requirement from an informal improvement idea?
files.watch: Point to each source role; emphasise that file 4 joins in Try 3 rather than the first prompt.

say: Scan the documents yourself and mark three kinds of information: what is confirmed, what someone suggests, and what the pack doesn't settle. Pay attention to preparation times, equipment, communication, and who can confirm readiness.

You don't need to memorise the files, but you do need enough familiarity to challenge the answer later. A missing contact or approver should stay visible as a question, not become a plausible name added for convenience.
read.ask: What is one requirement you can verify and one important detail the files leave unresolved?
read.watch: Give quiet scanning time; require a source reference for the confirmed item and avoid inventing a missing owner.

say: Open the work chat route shown and use its file picker to select the training documents for the question. Compare the selected file names with the pack rather than assuming that mentioning a title in ordinary text attached the file.

We'll use the first three files for the initial summary. If your interface uses a different selection control, we'll follow that route in your environment and check the resulting attachments before sending.
attach.ask: How will you confirm that the intended reference files are actually selected for this question?
attach.watch: Check visible selected-file chips or attachments; support the local picker without insisting on one universal interface.

say: Use Prompt 1 with the event brief, issues report, and handover notes to organise the context into four sections. We want requirements, observed problems, suggestions, and missing information kept apart.

This is a reading task in chat, not the moment to create the Word guide. Notice the instruction not to invent missing details, because a neat summary would be misleading if it supplied an approver or service time that the files don't confirm.
t1do.ask: Why would merging suggestions into the requirements section make the next drafting task riskier?
t1do.watch: Confirm files 1 to 3 only; wait for the learner's actual summary and keep the four requested categories visible.

say: Read your actual summary beside the checking questions and trace its important requirements to the files. The illustrated sections show a possible structure, not a guarantee that your response is complete or correct.

Look for the inspection, equipment, and organiser communication details, then inspect where the final approver and other gaps appear. The test is whether the answer separates those statuses honestly rather than whether it resembles the example's wording.
t1ok.ask: Where in your summary is an unresolved item clearly separated from a confirmed requirement?
t1ok.watch: Check one confirmed detail and one gap against the source; don't recite the illustrative card as the learner's result.

say: The scattered context has now been brought into a form you can inspect, which completes the first move. That doesn't yet make every line of the summary verified.

Keep your chat available, because the next prompt asks for the evidence behind the points you've just read. This checkpoint is simply a pause to notice the difference between collecting the information and proving that the interpretation respects the source files.
cp1.ask: Which point in your summary most needs an explicit source check next?
cp1.watch: Let learners retain the same chat; take a brief reflection rather than adding a new writing task.

say: Stay in the same chat and ask Prompt 2 to check the summary against the three references. Each major point needs a supporting file, a status, and any conflict or missing detail.

Give special attention to room-ready approval, catering times, escalation contacts, and equipment ownership. The prompt asks Copilot to expose uncertainty rather than resolve it, so we'll reject answers that turn an absence of evidence into a convenient assumption.
t2do.ask: Which of the highlighted operational details would be unsafe to fill in by guessing?
t2do.watch: Keep the original three references in context; inspect whether the response reports uncertainty rather than deciding it.

say: Use the evidence table in your real response to follow a major requirement back to its supporting file. A file name beside a sentence is a starting point for checking, not proof that the sentence is accurate.

Compare the status too: an observed problem isn't a policy, and a proposed improvement isn't a confirmed event requirement. Where multiple files leave something unresolved, preserve that uncertainty rather than choosing the answer that sounds most practical.
t2ok.ask: Does the status assigned to your chosen point match what its supporting file actually says?
t2ok.watch: Open the cited source for one row; check the statement and its status independently of the example table.

say: Add the fourth file, the draft conference checklist, and use Prompt 3 to compare it with the evidence you've already checked. Ask what should stay, what is vague or duplicated, what is missing, and what isn't supported.

We're deliberately stopping short of a rewrite here. Naming the weakness and a specific improvement gives us a clearer reason for the later guide than simply asking Copilot to make the old checklist better.
t3do.ask: What would a useful critique tell you that a polished rewrite alone would hide?
t3do.watch: Confirm the draft checklist is newly selected alongside files 1 to 3; stop unintended rewriting before the next stage.

say: Read the critique you received and test whether its proposed improvements follow from the source files. The screen's example about telling the organiser everything is ready illustrates why a short instruction can still carry an unsupported commitment.

Find what your critique recommends retaining as well as removing or clarifying. We aren't assuming every suggested fix is correct, and we shouldn't replace an uncertain approval route with another confident instruction that nobody has authorised.
t3ok.ask: How does your critique handle the checklist's instruction to communicate readiness when approval is unresolved?
t3ok.watch: Inspect the actual readiness critique; don't endorse a sample replacement as a newly approved hotel procedure.

say: We now have two kinds of checked material: a clearer view of the source evidence and a critique of the existing checklist. Together they tell us what the new guide needs to preserve, improve, and leave unresolved.
Pause before drafting and keep the supporting files intact. The next stage creates a separate output, so we can improve the team's working guide without rewriting the evidence we need to review it.
cp2.ask: What is one confirmed requirement and one weakness you'll carry into the new guide?
cp2.watch: Make sure learners have retained the references and critique; keep the checkpoint separate from the drafting prompt.

say: Create a new blank Word document and name it as your Conference Day Readiness Guide with your own name attached. This is the working output; the four source files remain unchanged.

Before we send the drafting prompt, notice how it defines the audience, purpose, evidence, structure, wording, and boundaries. Those details give the draft a useful operational shape while telling it what to do when the pack doesn't provide an answer.
blank.ask: What will distinguish your new working guide from the unchanged source checklist?
blank.watch: Check learners create a separate document; prevent edits to the original four source files.

say: Use Prompt 4 in the new Word document with all four reference files selected, following the editing route shown for your environment. We're asking for a concise guide that staff can use for preparation, checks, communication, escalation, and handover.

The prompt also requires missing owners, contacts, timings, and approvals to be marked as needing confirmation. Keep that instruction in place; an attractive draft must not hide the decisions the source pack leaves open.
t4do.ask: Which unresolved details must remain visible when the first guide is drafted?
t4do.watch: Check the selected editing mode and four references; confirm generation is in the new guide, not a source document.

say: Inspect the guide you actually received using the six questions, rather than treating the illustrated list of headings as a completed output. Check whether it preserves the confirmed requirements and makes unresolved items easy to spot.

Then read it as a colleague preparing the event: could you find the next action quickly, or would you have to interpret paragraphs under pressure? The first draft is material for improvement, not a final operational instruction.
t4ok.ask: Which part of your draft is hardest to use quickly, and is that a structure problem or a missing-information problem?
t4ok.watch: Inspect real draft content for unsupported owners and promises; distinguish concise formatting from verified accuracy.

say: Compare your draft with a partner's and focus on whether the structure helps someone do the work. Different wording is expected, so don't try to decide which document matches the illustration most closely.

Choose a section in each guide and look for clear actions, preserved requirements, and visible gaps. A useful comparison gives you a specific improvement to make, not merely a preference for one heading style or a longer-looking document.
compare.ask: What is one structural choice in your partner's guide that would make your own easier to use?
compare.watch: Compare only training outputs; steer discussion away from fonts and toward actions, evidence, and unresolved details.

say: Use Prompt 5 to improve the working guide's usability while preserving its verified meaning and open items. Ask for action-based headings, shorter passages, suitable checklists, and a practical order for preparation.

Watch what gets lost as well as what becomes easier to scan. An owner, deadline, escalation point, or confirmation label can be important even when it takes space, so brevity is not permission to remove the boundaries that make the guide honest.
t5do.ask: What detail must survive even if Copilot shortens your guide substantially?
t5do.watch: Compare the revised guide with the prior draft; watch for lost times, equipment, and confirmation labels.

say: Now make one improvement yourself in the Word document, using what you noticed during the comparison or review. Choose a change that helps a colleague act, such as clarifying a heading, removing repetition, or making an unresolved detail easier to see.

Be able to explain the reason for your edit rather than changing something only to complete the exercise. This is your working guide, and direct editing is part of taking responsibility for its usefulness.
edit.ask: What manual change did you make, and how will it help someone preparing the conference?
edit.watch: Require one genuine learner edit; do not substitute another Copilot prompt for this ownership step.

say: You have a guide that has been drafted, improved, and edited by you, but we haven't completed the final source check yet. A clearer document can still contain an unsupported instruction or omit a confirmed requirement.
Keep your current version open so the next exercise can review the actual guide. This pause marks progress in the writing process, not approval for colleagues to rely on the document.
cp3.ask: Which part of your improved guide would you most want checked against the references?
cp3.watch: Confirm the working version is saved or retained; avoid calling it verified before Try 6.

say: Select all four references again and use Prompt 6 to review the current guide against them. We're requesting a short correction list, not another automatic rewrite.

The check covers omissions, unsupported statements, suggestions presented as facts, missing confirmation labels, vague duplication, and premature readiness wording. Keeping corrections separate lets you inspect the evidence behind each recommendation before deciding what to change in the document.
t6do.ask: Why is a correction list more useful here than silently replacing the whole guide?
t6do.watch: Confirm the current guide and four references are in scope; stop automatic rewriting if it replaces the requested correction list.

say: Read each correction in your real response and verify it against the guide and the cited source before applying it. The example list shows possible defects, but it doesn't mean those defects exist in your document.

Accept the supported corrections and question anything that introduces a new assumption. Pay particular attention to who may declare readiness, because polished wording can still imply approval that the files never supplied.
t6ok.ask: Which correction will you apply, and what evidence makes it valid for your guide?
t6ok.watch: Do not assert sample defects are present; inspect one accepted correction and one recommendation needing verification.

say: The guide has now been through a source-based review, with you deciding which corrections to apply. Keep any remaining unresolved detail visible rather than treating the review as evidence that every operational decision is settled.

Our final move reuses the checked content in another format. Before that demonstration, notice that the wording and boundaries of the guide are the content we want to carry forward, not the original weak checklist.
cp4.ask: What unresolved detail must remain visible even after the guide has been reviewed?
cp4.watch: Pause for outstanding corrections; identify the reviewed guide as the source for visual reuse.

say: These six risks explain why we didn't stop at the first draft: invented approvers or contacts, suggestions turned into policy, premature readiness, missing requirements, and unnecessary length. Each can look reasonable in fluent prose.

Choose the risk most relevant to your guide and connect it to a concrete check you've made. If the problem is length, shorten the explanation without removing the times, ownership questions, escalation needs, or approval boundaries.
mistakes.ask: Which of these risks did you find or guard against in your own guide?
mistakes.watch: Link risks to learner evidence rather than claiming every defect occurred; show the fix prompt only for excessive length.

say: Watch the demonstration of turning the reviewed guide into a staff quick-reference visual using Prompt 7. The six areas on screen give the visual a simple shape, but its content must still come from the guide we've checked.

A shorter label can accidentally lose an important qualification, so we'll review meaning as well as readability. The illustrated poster is not a guaranteed result, and a real generated visual still needs checks for missing details and unsupported procedures.
create.ask: What important qualification could be lost when a guide instruction becomes a short visual label?
create.watch: Use the reviewed guide as source; treat the poster as illustrative and check real output text and approval wording.

say: For the two-minute challenge, choose the final check, issue-recovery, or handover section and replace the bracketed title in Prompt 8 with your choice. Ask for a concise addition supported by the current guide and the four files.

Inspect the addition before keeping it, especially where the sources leave a procedure or owner unresolved. If we need the time for correcting the main guide, we'll skip this extension rather than rush the review that makes it usable.
challenge.ask: Which section did you choose, and where did its new wording need a confirmation label?
challenge.watch: Run a real two-minute timer if used; ensure the placeholder is replaced and no new policy is invented.

say: We moved from mixed source notes to a guide by separating evidence, critiquing the draft, creating a new output, and improving it without losing the important boundaries. The visual demonstration reused that checked content rather than creating a new set of instructions.

The durable skill is preserving meaning while changing structure and format. A colleague should be able to see both what to do and what still needs confirmation, without having to guess which statements were trustworthy.
recap.ask: Which move most improved the reliability of your guide, rather than just its appearance?
recap.watch: Connect the recap to actual learner work; distinguish the reviewed guide from the illustrative visual.

say: Keep the eight prompts and the length-reduction fix as a record of this workflow. Notice that some prompts analyse or critique while others draft, improve, verify, or reuse; they aren't interchangeable requests to write something.

When you adapt the pack, keep the source roles and uncertainty instructions that made this exercise useful. Downloading the prompts helps you repeat the process, but every new document still needs its own evidence checks and human edits.
pack.ask: Which prompt would you use to check an existing guide before asking for a rewrite?
pack.watch: Show the individual copy route and complete download; distinguish the critique, drafting, and verification prompts.

say: You've practised combining documents, checking evidence, challenging a weak draft, writing a usable guide, and reusing reviewed content. The manual edit and correction decisions are as important as generating the first version.

For your next task, choose a small document where clearer actions and visible uncertainty would help colleagues. Bring the habits of preserving confirmed meaning, marking gaps, and owning the final wording rather than measuring success by how quickly a draft appears.
learned.ask: What document would you improve next, and how would you stop suggestions from becoming unsupported instructions?
learned.watch: Close with one concrete next use; remind learners the fictional guide is not approved real hotel policy.
